summary:
Guam stands under the full United States federal framework as an unincorporated United States territory. United States passports and other federal travel documents reflect sex assigned at birth, and the X gender marker was eliminated by a January 2025 executive order, so a trans visitor travelling on United States documents faces a mismatch between document and presentation at entry.

Screening at Guam's airport follows Transport Security Administration procedure, which applies in Guam as a United States territory. The agency's body-scanner and pat-down protocols can disclose a trans traveller's status to officers. Travellers may request an alternative screening method and escalate problems on the spot, and most trans travellers pass screening without incident. Guidance for trans travellers also addresses pre-flight packing and handling document and screening mismatches.

The January 2025 executive order halting federal funding for gender-affirming care reaches federally funded institutions in Guam, so access to that care during a visit can be constrained by federal policy rather than local practice.

A separate January 2025 executive order bans transgender troops from serving openly and directs the Secretary of Defense to submit an implementation plan within 30 days; the order frames trans identity as "radical gender ideology." It applies in Guam, which hosts a large permanent United States military presence, and indicates the federal posture a visitor can expect from official institutions on the island.

On partner recognition, chief judge Frances M Tydingco-Gatewood struck down Guam's prohibition on same-sex marriage in June 2015 following an April 2015 lawsuit by Loretta Pangelinan and Kathleen Aguero, who had been denied a marriage licence. The ruling took effect at 8am on Tuesday 9 June 2015, making Guam the first United States territory to recognise same-sex marriage.
tangentialFactors:
Guam holds a distinct place in the regional pattern of relationship recognition: it became the first United States territory to recognise same-sex marriage, ahead of the territory status generally associated with that change.

The island hosts a large permanent United States military presence, so federal personnel policy, including the January 2025 order barring open transgender service, is unusually visible in local institutions and in the surrounding public culture.

Federal executive action rather than the Guam Legislature is the principal driver of trans-related policy conditions on the island, which means a visitor's exposure to screening, care access, and official framing tracks Washington decisions made in January 2025.
localsOnly:
Guam residents marry under a local marriage statute that has permitted same-sex marriage since the June 2015 ruling by the Guam federal court, and Guam's licensing authorities issue marriage licences to same-sex couples on the same basis as opposite-sex couples.

Residents who serve in the United States military on island are subject to the January 2025 federal order on open transgender service, with an implementation plan directed to the Secretary of Defense within 30 days of the order.

Residents seeking gender-affirming care at federally funded institutions in Guam are affected by the January 2025 order halting that funding, which operates through federal policy rather than through Guam law.

Guam residents travelling on United States passports carry sex-assignment markers rather than an X marker, since the X option was eliminated by executive order in January 2025.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Guam's local government amends birth certificates or driver's licences with a changed gender marker is unresolved in the material consulted; the sources address federal documents and airport screening but not Guam-specific identity-document practice.

Guam's own anti-discrimination statute and any territory-level hate-crime protection covering gender identity were not sourced in this pass and remain unresolved.

Two sources in the inventory, one on Pacific sexual identity and one on Guam identity documents, yielded no usable finding, so claims about local legal aid routes or territory-specific document procedures cannot be verified from them.

Enforcement data on how often airport screening results in an outging or a complaint at Guam's airport is not sourced; the available guidance states only that most trans travellers pass screening without incident.
